title: TCP Fast Open
summary: This experimental document describes TCP Fast Open, which allows data in SYN and SYN-ACK packets, consumed during the handshake, saving up to one round trip. TFO deviates from standard TCP behavior.

plainLanguage.summary: Normally you say hello before talking. TCP Fast Open lets you pass along your first message while saying hello, saving a trip back and forth.

questions: how to send data in syn
how does tcp fast open work
subtitle: Let a returning client put its first request inside the TCP SYN packet and save a round trip.

tldr.problem: Standard TCP cannot exchange data until its three-way handshake finishes, which adds one round-trip time to every new connection. For short web transfers that delay is a large share of total latency.
tldr.mechanism: The server hands the client a Fast Open Cookie, a MAC tag that authenticates the client's IP address. On later connections the client sends data in the SYN together with the cookie, and the server delivers that data to the application at once if the cookie is valid.
tldr.outcome: TFO can save up to one full round-trip time, but data in a SYN can be replayed to the application in rare cases, so applications must tolerate duplicates before enabling it. The RFC is Experimental.

today: RFC 7413 is an Experimental RFC. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and the text itself says TFO deviates from standard TCP semantics, so applications should use it only if they can tolerate replayed SYN data.

sections.title: Why Data in the SYN
sections.content:
TCP Fast Open (TFO) is an experimental update to TCP that lets data be exchanged safely during the connection handshake. Current TCP only permits data after the three-way handshake (3WHS) from RFC 793, which adds one round-trip time (RTT) to latency.

The RFC is motivated by the web. It notes that the Chrome browser keeps TCP connections idle for up to 5 minutes, yet 35% of HTTP requests are still made on new TCP connections. For such applications, placing data in the SYN can give significant latency improvements.
sections.plainLanguage: Saying hello and waiting for an answer before you speak takes time. If you can slip your question into the hello, you get your answer sooner.

sections.title: Two Problems with Data in SYN
sections.content:
Standard TCP already allows data in a SYN, but forbids the receiver from delivering it to the application until the 3WHS completes, because the handshake is how TCP catches old or duplicate SYNs. TFO removes that constraint, which raises two issues.

  • Duplicate SYNs. Data in a duplicate SYN could be delivered twice, for example if the receiver rebooted and forgot the original SYN, or if the duplicate arrives after a connection closed by the sender (so TIME-WAIT no longer protects it). The designers chose to accept this and restrict TFO to applications that tolerate duplicate SYN data. The now obsoleted T/TCP (RFC 1644) tried to solve this and was not deployed because of vulnerabilities.
  • Spoofed addresses. SYNs with spoofed source addresses can already cause a SYN flood (RFC 4987). With TFO the server would pass data up to the application, wasting CPU and memory and enabling amplified reflection attacks if the response is larger than the request. None of the usual SYN flood mitigations apply, so TFO uses a server-supplied cookie.

Because of these issues, TCP implementations MUST NOT use TFO by default. They use it only when an application requests it explicitly, on a per-service-port basis.
sections.plainLanguage: Skipping the hello check means a repeated message might be heard twice, and a stranger could pretend to be someone else to cause trouble. So TFO is only turned on when a program asks for it.

sections.title: How a Fast Open Connection Works
sections.content:
The key component is the Fast Open Cookie, a message authentication code (MAC) tag generated by the server. It takes two connections to benefit.

First, the client requests a cookie. It sends a SYN with a Fast Open option and an empty cookie field. The server generates a cookie and returns it in the Fast Open option of the SYN-ACK. The client caches it.

Later, the client performs TFO. It sends a SYN carrying data and the cookie. If the cookie is valid, the server acknowledges both the SYN and the data, and delivers the data to the application. Otherwise it drops the data and acknowledges only the SYN sequence number. A server that accepts the data may send response data before the handshake finishes, up to the limit set by TCP congestion control (RFC 5681).

The client then sends an ACK. If its data was not acknowledged, it retransmits that data in the ACK, so there is no latency penalty when the server declines. From there the connection proceeds like normal TCP. The client can repeat Fast Open many times until the server expires the cookie, so TFO suits applications with temporal locality between a client and a server.
sections.plainLanguage: The first visit, the server gives you a pass. Next time you show the pass along with your question right away. If the pass is no good, you just ask again a moment later, like normal.

sections.title: The Cookie and the Fast Open Option
sections.content:
The Fast Open option has a Kind of 34 and a Length from 6 to 18 bytes, which must be even. The cookie is either empty or 4 to 16 bytes. Options with invalid Length values, or without the SYN flag set, MUST be ignored. A cookie request is a SYN with a Length field of 0 for the cookie.

The server generates and checks cookies. The cookie SHOULD authenticate the client's source IP address, be impossible for anyone but the server to fabricate, be fast to generate and verify, and expire after a time, for example through key rotation or a timestamp. The server needs two operations, GetCookie(IP_Address) and IsCookieValid(IP_Address, Cookie). A simple example in the RFC encrypts the IP address with AES_128 and truncates the result to 64 bits.

The client MUST cache cookies, at most one per client and server IP address pair, and it is recommended to cache the server's MSS too, since the SYN is sent before the server announces its MSS. Without a cached MSS, SYN data is limited to the default 536 bytes for IPv4 or 1220 bytes for IPv6. The client MUST also cache negative responses (data not acknowledged, ICMP errors, or no reply at all) and SHOULD disable Fast Open on that path at least temporarily, because incompatible middleboxes might otherwise block it forever.
sections.plainLanguage: The pass is a short secret code that only the server can make. The server can change the rules so old passes stop working, and your computer remembers which servers did not like the trick.

sections.title: Security and Server Defenses
sections.content:
The cookie stops an attacker from trivially flooding spoofed SYNs with data. Even so, the server keeps a FastOpenEnabled flag, which is off by default and MUST be turned on by the application, and a PendingFastOpenRequests counter. If the counter goes over a preset system limit, the server MUST disable TFO for new connections until it drops, so requests fall back to regular handshakes and SYN flood defenses such as SYN cookies can work.

The RFC discusses residual risks. An attacker with valid cookies from compromised hosts can still flood spoofed SYNs with data. An attacker behind a NAT can obtain valid cookies that work for others behind the same address. An attacker who obtains cookies and then releases a DHCP-assigned address could cause servers to send data to the victim who gets that address next. The best defense against amplification is for the server not to respond with data until the handshake finishes, at the cost of some of the latency saving.
sections.plainLanguage: A pass cannot stop every trick, so servers count how many half-open visitors they have. If there are too many, they stop accepting early questions until things calm down.

sections.title: When to Use TFO
sections.content:
Replay is the main concern. A client that cannot handle receiving the same SYN data more than once MUST NOT enable TFO to send data in a SYN, and a server that cannot accept it MUST NOT enable TFO to receive it. The RFC suggests that a POST without application-level protection is a poor fit for the SYN, while GET requests are well suited. Putting a TLS client_hello in the SYN is safe and saves one RTT in the TLS handshake.

To benefit, the first application data unit must fit in a single segment. Applications SHOULD still reuse connections where possible. Servers behind load balancers should share a key so that they generate identical cookies for a given client address.

Open questions include middleboxes (studies cited found that 6% of probed paths drop SYNs with data or unknown options, so TFO falls back to a plain SYN after a timeout), interaction with congestion control, and a cookie-less variant for servers that are immune to the attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: It is great for short, repeatable questions like asking for a web page, and a bad idea for something you must only do once, like paying a bill.

messages.note: Acknowledges the SYN and the data when the cookie is valid.

messages.note: Response data may be sent before the handshake finishes.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: 1 byte; 6 to 18, and the number must be even.

fields.name: Cookie
fields.desc: 0, or 4 to 16 bytes (Length minus 2); shown here as a variable-length field.
